Migrating from Robyn

Source: vignettes/articles/migrating-from-robyn.Rmd
migrating-from-robyn.Rmd

This article is for an analyst with a Robyn model who wants to reproduce it, or build on it, with mediamix. Robyn, Meta’s open-source marketing mix modelling package, adstocks and saturates each channel, fits a ridge regression, and searches the transform parameters and the penalty with the Python library Nevergrad. mediamix implements the same geometric, Weibull and Hill transforms as plain R functions, and from_robyn() converts a channel’s Robyn hyperparameters into arguments that reproduce the series Robyn fitted on. From there every reporting and planning function in mediamix runs on Robyn’s regressors, with Robyn’s coefficients or with those of a model you fit yourself.

Statements about Robyn here come from its R source (Zhou et al., 2025) on the main branch of facebookexperimental/Robyn at commit 5915aa9 (version 3.12.1, June 2025), in the files transformation.R, model.R, allocator.R, inputs.R, pareto.R, clusters.R, calibration.R and refresh.R under R/R/. Where a rule changed between releases, the release tags are named.

How the pieces correspond

Robyn mediamix Notes
Geometric adstock, theta adstock_geometric() with decay = theta and normalise = FALSE Exact; from_robyn() converts it
Weibull CDF adstock, shape and scale adstock_weibull() with type = "cdf" and normalise = FALSE Exact once scale is converted to periods, which from_robyn() does
Weibull PDF adstock adstock_filter() with Robyn’s kernel as weights No adstock_weibull() arguments reproduce it
Hill alpha and gamma saturate_hill() with shape = alpha and the converted half_max Exact given the series and the window; the rule for half_max depends on the Robyn version
Modelling window Transform every row, then use the window’s rows; window in from_robyn() Exact
Decomposition (xDecompAgg) contributions() Same products; non-media terms pooled into "(baseline)"
roi_total roi() Same definition
The allocator’s marginal response marginal_roi() A different definition
robyn_response() response_curve(), simulate_plan()
robyn_allocator() allocate_budget() A different method
Ridge regression with glmnet glmnet::glmnet() with alpha = 0 on the transformed columns mediamix fits no model
Nevergrad search tune_carryover_joint() for the decays; step_adstock_channels() and step_saturation() with tune for the rest One objective instead of two or three
Prophet trend, season and holiday terms fourier_terms(), holiday_flags() and a week counter, as controls A different method
Calibration, Pareto fronts, clustering, refresh None

Reproducing Robyn’s transformed series

Robyn::run_transformations() adstocks every row of InputCollect$dt_mod, then saturates the rows of the modelling window, computing the Hill inflexion point from those rows. from_robyn() therefore needs the channel’s column of dt_mod in date order, its hyperparameters, and the window as row positions, rollingWindowStartWhich:rollingWindowEndWhich in InputCollect.

Suppose a Robyn model of weekly revenue in the north geography of mm_weekly, with geometric adstock and a modelling window starting on 3 July 2023, the 27th week, had chosen these hyperparameters for television and search:

library(mediamix)
data(mm_weekly)
north <- mm_weekly[mm_weekly$geo == "north", ]
north <- north[order(north$date), ]
window <- which(north$date >= as.Date("2023-07-03"))

robyn_hyp <- list(tv_thetas = 0.6, tv_alphas = 2.2, tv_gammas = 0.5,
                  search_thetas = 0.1, search_alphas = 1.1,
                  search_gammas = 0.4)

Each channel converts in one call:

channels <- c(tv = "tv", search = "search")
args <- lapply(channels, function(ch) {
  from_robyn(north[[ch]],
             theta = robyn_hyp[[paste0(ch, "_thetas")]],
             alpha = robyn_hyp[[paste0(ch, "_alphas")]],
             gamma = robyn_hyp[[paste0(ch, "_gammas")]],
             window = window)
})
str(args$tv)
#> List of 2
#>  $ adstock   :List of 3
#>   ..$ kernel   : chr "geometric"
#>   ..$ decay    : num 0.6
#>   ..$ normalise: logi FALSE
#>  $ saturation:List of 3
#>   ..$ type    : chr "hill"
#>   ..$ half_max: num 3213
#>   ..$ shape   : num 2.2

theta becomes the geometric decay, with normalise = FALSE because Robyn accumulates the unnormalised recursion at=xt+θat−1a_t = x_t + \theta a_{t-1} from a1=x1a_1 = x_1. alpha becomes the shape of the Hill curve (Hill, 1910). gamma becomes half_max, an amount of adstocked media: the inflexion point Robyn computed from this series. half_life() reads a theta as a half-life in weeks:

half_life(c(tv = 0.6, search = 0.1))
#>     tv search 
#>  1.357  0.301

To check the conversion without Robyn, the next chunk re-creates the two functions Robyn applies, Robyn::adstock_geometric() and Robyn::saturation_hill(), from R/R/transformation.R at commit 5915aa9 (the file last changed in commit 33baf19, June 2025). They are reduced to the values compared here, and Robyn’s names are written in snake_case, as in the package’s tests.

# Robyn's adstock_geometric(): the unnormalised recursion, from a_1 = x_1.
robyn_geometric <- function(x, theta) {
  x_decayed <- c(x[1], rep(0, length(x) - 1))
  for (xi in 2:length(x_decayed)) {
    x_decayed[xi] <- x[xi] + theta * x_decayed[xi - 1]
  }
  x_decayed
}

# Robyn's saturation_hill() from 3.12.0: the inflexion point is gamma times
# the largest adstocked value in the window.
robyn_hill <- function(x, alpha, gamma) {
  inflexion <- max(x) * gamma
  x**alpha / (x**alpha + inflexion**alpha)
}

Robyn adstocks the whole series and saturates the window’s rows; media_transform() with the converted arguments transforms every row, and the two agree on every row of the window:

difference <- vapply(channels, function(ch) {
  adstocked <- robyn_geometric(north[[ch]], robyn_hyp[[paste0(ch, "_thetas")]])
  robyn <- robyn_hill(adstocked[window],
                      alpha = robyn_hyp[[paste0(ch, "_alphas")]],
                      gamma = robyn_hyp[[paste0(ch, "_gammas")]])
  ours <- media_transform(north[[ch]], adstock = args[[ch]]$adstock,
                          saturation = args[[ch]]$saturation)[window]
  max(abs(ours - robyn))
}, numeric(1))
difference
#>        tv    search 
#> 2.220e-16 1.665e-16

The largest difference, on a scale from 0 to 1, is rounding error.

The Hill inflexion point depends on the Robyn version

Robyn’s gamma places the inflexion point relative to the adstocked series in the window, and the rule changed in release 3.12.0. From 3.12.0, Robyn::saturation_hill() puts the point at gamma times the largest adstocked value in the window. Releases 3.7.0 to 3.11.1 interpolated within the window’s range instead, (1 - gamma) * min + gamma * max. The two rules agree when the adstocked series reaches zero inside the window. Search runs every week here, so its adstocked series never does, and the older rule moves its half_max:

old <- from_robyn(north$search, theta = 0.1, alpha = 1.1, gamma = 0.4,
                  window = window, inflexion = "range")
c(robyn_3.12 = args$search$saturation$half_max,
  robyn_3.11 = old$saturation$half_max)
#> robyn_3.12 robyn_3.11 
#>      372.4      527.1

Set inflexion = "range" for a model fitted by Robyn 3.7.0 to 3.11.1. Releases 3.0.0 to 3.6.3 computed the same range point as a quantile of 100 evenly spaced values between the minimum and the maximum, rounded to four decimal places, so for their models "range" gives the inflexion point to that rounding. From 3.12.0 Robyn also stores the inflexion point each channel used, in OutputCollect$resultHypParam, in a column named after the channel with _inflexion appended. A converted half_max equal to it confirms that the series, the window and the version all match.

Weibull adstock

Robyn measures the Weibull scale as a share of the series length and converts it to periods as round(quantile(1:n, scale)), where n is the number of rows it adstocks; its CDF kernel spans all n lags and starts at a weight of 1. from_robyn() makes the same conversion, so one scale means a longer carryover on a longer series:

w156 <- from_robyn(north$tv, adstock = "weibull_cdf", shape = 1.2,
                   scale = 0.04)
w104 <- from_robyn(north$tv[1:104], adstock = "weibull_cdf", shape = 1.2,
                   scale = 0.04)
c(periods_from_156_rows = w156$adstock$scale,
  periods_from_104_rows = w104$adstock$scale)
#> periods_from_156_rows periods_from_104_rows 
#>                     7                     5

The same check as before, against Robyn::adstock_weibull() with type = "cdf", its dplyr::lag() written in base R:

robyn_weibull_cdf <- function(x, shape, scale) {
  windlen <- length(x)
  x_bin <- 1:windlen
  scale_trans <- round(quantile(1:windlen, scale), 0)
  theta_vec <- c(1, 1 - pweibull(head(x_bin, -1), shape = shape,
                                 scale = scale_trans))
  theta_vec_cum <- cumprod(theta_vec)
  x_decayed <- mapply(function(x_val, x_pos) {
    x_vec <- c(rep(0, x_pos - 1), rep(x_val, windlen - x_pos + 1))
    lagged <- c(rep(0, x_pos - 1), theta_vec_cum)[seq_len(windlen)]
    x_vec * lagged
  }, x_val = x, x_pos = seq_along(x))
  rowSums(x_decayed)
}

ours <- media_transform(north$tv, adstock = w156$adstock, saturation = NULL)
max(abs(ours - robyn_weibull_cdf(north$tv, shape = 1.2, scale = 0.04)))
#> [1] 5.457e-12

The difference is again rounding error, here on adstocked values in the thousands. From release 3.10.0 a shape or scale of 0 switches Robyn’s Weibull carryover off, and from_robyn() then returns kernel = "none".

Robyn’s PDF form rescales the Weibull density over its n lags so that the smallest weight is 0 and the largest 1. adstock_weibull() divides by the largest weight only, so no adstock_weibull() arguments reproduce Robyn’s series, and from_robyn() refuses adstock = "weibull_pdf" rather than return an approximation. adstock_filter() applies Robyn’s kernel when it is given as weights, and the package’s tests check the result against Robyn’s series:

n <- nrow(north)
d <- dweibull(1:n, shape = 2.5, scale = round(quantile(1:n, 0.1)))
robyn_pdf_kernel <- (d - min(d)) / (max(d) - min(d))
tv_pdf <- adstock_filter(north$tv, weights = robyn_pdf_kernel)

The modelling window

Robyn fits its model on the window’s rows only, but adstocks from the first row of dt_mod, so the weeks before the window give its first weeks their carryover; its documentation of window_start recommends not starting the window on the first date for that reason. In mediamix, transform the whole series and pass only the window’s rows to the model, to contributions() and to roi(). Without earlier weeks to draw on, adstock_steady_state() gives the filter a starting state instead.

Bringing a fitted Robyn model across

A Robyn model’s hyperparameters are in OutputCollect$resultHypParam and its coefficients in OutputCollect$xDecompAgg, one set per solID; Robyn’s own allocator reads them from there. The code below needs a Robyn model and was not run here. It converts every paid channel, checks the inflexion points and reports the returns, assuming each channel was modelled on its spend rather than on an exposure metric such as impressions, so that its column of dt_mod holds spend.

sol <- "1_210_4"   # the solID of the model you chose
hyp <- as.data.frame(OutputCollect$resultHypParam)
hyp <- hyp[hyp$solID == sol, ]
decomp <- as.data.frame(OutputCollect$xDecompAgg)
decomp <- decomp[decomp$solID == sol, ]
coefs <- stats::setNames(decomp$coef, decomp$rn)

dt <- as.data.frame(InputCollect$dt_mod)
window <- with(InputCollect, rollingWindowStartWhich:rollingWindowEndWhich)
paid <- InputCollect$paid_media_selected

spec <- lapply(stats::setNames(paid, paid), function(ch) {
  h <- function(p) hyp[[paste0(ch, "_", p)]]
  if (InputCollect$adstock == "geometric") {
    from_robyn(dt[[ch]], theta = h("thetas"), alpha = h("alphas"),
               gamma = h("gammas"), window = window)
  } else {
    from_robyn(dt[[ch]], adstock = InputCollect$adstock,
               shape = h("shapes"), scale = h("scales"),
               alpha = h("alphas"), gamma = h("gammas"), window = window)
  }
})

# Each converted half_max should equal the inflexion point Robyn stored
cbind(mediamix = sapply(spec, function(s) s$saturation$half_max),
      robyn = unlist(hyp[paste0(paid, "_inflexion")]))

media <- transform_plan(dt, spec)[window, ]
contrib <- contributions(media[paid], coefs[c("(Intercept)", paid)],
                         index = media$ds)
roi(contrib, dt[window, paid])
marginal_roi(dt, coefs, spec = spec, rows = window)

contributions() gets a bare coefficient vector here, so its "(baseline)" is Robyn’s intercept alone, while its media rows are Robyn’s media decomposition. With rows, marginal_roi() raises spend in the window only. For a model from Robyn 3.7.0 to 3.11.1, take the channels from InputCollect$paid_media_spends, since paid_media_selected arrived in 3.12.0, add inflexion = "range" to the from_robyn() calls, and drop the comparison with the stored inflexion points, which those releases do not keep.

Reporting

Robyn’s decomposition multiplies each regressor by its coefficient over the window, keeping the intercept, each Prophet term and each control as a separate line, and splits every channel’s effect into immediate and carryover parts. contributions() makes the same products for the media columns and pools everything else into "(baseline)"; it has no immediate and carryover split. Robyn’s roi_total divides a channel’s total effect in the window by its total spend there, which is what roi() computes from the same rows.

The marginal returns differ. Robyn’s allocator evaluates each channel’s Hill curve at its mean spend per period plus its mean historical carryover, and takes the change in that one period’s response when the mean spend rises by one unit. marginal_roi() raises spend by 1% in every period, re-runs carryover and saturation over the whole series and divides the extra response by the extra spend, the definition of Jin et al. (2017), so carryover into later weeks and the spread of weekly spend both count.

robyn_response() returns a channel’s response to a given level of spend. response_curve() traces a fitted curve across levels of adstocked media, with its marginal return at each, and simulate_plan() gives the response to a whole weekly plan through the transforms.

Budget allocation

robyn_allocator() and allocate_budget() both split a budget across channels to maximise the predicted response, in different ways.

  • Robyn works with each channel’s mean spend per period over date_range, adds the mean historical carryover, and evaluates the Hill curve at that single point. allocate_budget() rescales each channel’s whole weekly series and runs carryover and saturation week by week, so flighting and the carryover between weeks enter the response.
  • Robyn optimises with nloptr’s augmented Lagrangian method around a local, gradient-based search, SLSQP by default or MMA. allocate_budget() evaluates every channel on a grid of steps increments and picks the best combination by dynamic programming, which handles S-shaped curves and is only as fine as the grid.
  • Robyn’s channel_constr_low and channel_constr_up are multiples of each channel’s mean spend; allocate_budget()’s lower and upper are total spend.
  • Robyn also has a target_efficiency scenario, which looks for the spend that meets a target ROAS or CPA, and by default leaves out channels whose coefficient is 0. allocate_budget() splits a given total only.

allocate_budget() rescales every row of the plan it is given, so give it the weeks being planned. Both answers rest on curves that are identified only over the spend levels in the data.

Fitting the model

mediamix has no model of its own. Robyn’s internal model_refit() calls glmnet::glmnet() with family = "gaussian" and alpha = 0, a ridge regression (Hoerl and Kennard, 1970; Friedman et al., 2010), at a lambda that its search chooses between bounds computed from the data. Paid media coefficients have a lower limit of 0 by default (paid_media_signs = "positive"), and when the intercept comes out negative Robyn refits without one (intercept_sign = "non_negative", the default). With ts_validation = TRUE it splits the window into training, validation and test sets by a train_size hyperparameter. A refit outside Robyn can make the same glmnet::glmnet() call on the transformed columns, or use any other model.

Choosing the hyperparameters

Robyn searches every hyperparameter at once with Nevergrad (Rapin and Teytaud, 2018), TwoPointsDE by default, reached through reticulate. It scores each candidate on NRMSE, the model’s fit error, and DECOMP.RSSD, the distance between each channel’s share of the media effect and its share of spend, with MAPE against experiments as a third objective when it is calibrating. mediamix has no multi-objective search.

tune_carryover_joint() chooses each channel’s geometric decay and kernel length by forward-only cross-validation of one model holding every channel and the controls, on a single metric, RMSE by default; it does not tune saturation. For carryover, saturation and the ridge penalty together, a tidymodels workflow tunes step_adstock_channels() and step_saturation() alongside a glmnet model. The code below needs the tune, parsnip, workflows, yardstick, rsample and glmnet packages and was not run here:

library(recipes)
library(parsnip)
library(workflows)
library(tune)

media_cols <- c("tv", "video", "search", "social", "display")
rec <- recipe(revenue ~ ., data = north) |>
  update_role(date, new_role = "index") |>
  step_rm(geo) |>
  step_adstock_channels(media_cols, index = "date", decay = tune(),
                        normalise = FALSE) |>
  step_saturation(all_of(media_cols), half_max = tune(), shape = tune()) |>
  step_normalize(all_numeric_predictors())

ridge <- linear_reg(penalty = tune(), mixture = 0) |> set_engine("glmnet")
wf <- workflow() |> add_recipe(rec) |> add_model(ridge)
folds <- rsample::rolling_origin(north, initial = 104, assess = 13,
                                 skip = 12, cumulative = TRUE)
res <- tune_bayes(wf, resamples = folds, initial = 10, iter = 20)

step_adstock_channels() gives each channel a decay of its own. With ref = "max", the default, step_saturation() sets half_max as a fraction of the largest adstocked value in the training data, the same idea as Robyn’s gamma from 3.12.0, and its shape is Robyn’s alpha. One step_saturation() shares those two values across the columns it selects; Robyn’s per-channel alpha and gamma need a step per channel, each with its own tune() ids. vignette("tidymodels") covers the steps in detail.

What has no counterpart

  • Calibration. Robyn’s calibration_input takes lift-test results and adds the error against them as an objective, and the experimental robyn_calibrate() fits a Hill curve to spend and response data. mediamix calibrates nothing; an experiment can still check its answers.
  • Model selection. Robyn keeps the candidates on its Pareto fronts of NRMSE and DECOMP.RSSD (robyn_pareto()), groups them by k-means (robyn_clusters()) and reports intervals from bootstrapping the ROIs of the models in each cluster. mediamix’s tuners return one choice on one metric, and block_bootstrap() puts intervals on one model by resampling blocks of weeks, which measures sampling variation rather than the spread between candidate models.
  • Prophet terms. Robyn fits Prophet (Taylor and Letham, 2018) to the dependent variable and enters its trend, season and holiday components as regressors. mediamix builds calendar controls directly with fourier_terms() and holiday_flags().
  • Refreshing a model. robyn_refresh() rebuilds a selected model on new data, with hyperparameter bounds set around the old values. mediamix has no equivalent; step_adstock() continues the carryover filter into new weeks, but the model is refitted by you.
